text: A manager receives with \(\mathrm{MPI\_ANY\_SOURCE}\) as the source. After the call, it reads {{c1::\(\mathrm{status.MPI\_SOURCE}\)}} to learn which rank sent the message, and {{c2::\(\mathrm{status.MPI\_TAG}\)}} to learn its tag.
extra: MPI does not overwrite the source argument you passed in. The sender's rank is only in the \(\mathrm{MPI\_Status}\) struct, which has at least the members \(\mathrm{MPI\_SOURCE}\), \(\mathrm{MPI\_TAG}\) and \(\mathrm{MPI\_ERROR}\).

text: The count you pass to \(\mathrm{MPI\_Recv}\) is only the buffer capacity. To get the number of elements that arrived, the receiver calls {{c1::\(\mathrm{MPI\_Get\_count}\)}} with the status and the receive datatype.
extra: The count is not a member of the status struct because it depends on the datatype. It is the bytes received divided by the bytes per element, so MPI computes it only when you ask.

text: \(\mathrm{MPI\_Send}\) and \(\mathrm{MPI\_Recv}\) return {{c1::an error code}}, which is {{c2::\(\mathrm{MPI\_SUCCESS}\)}} on success. They do not return the number of elements received.
extra: This is the trap in study guide practice question 2. The element count comes from \(\mathrm{MPI\_Get\_count}\).

text: Workers finish in an unpredictable order. If rank 0 receives in rank order, it {{c1::blocks on a slow worker}} while finished results wait. With {{c2::\(\mathrm{MPI\_ANY\_SOURCE}\)}} it takes results in the order the workers finish.
extra: A2 uses this for its work queue. The manager receives each request with \(\mathrm{MPI\_ANY\_SOURCE}\) and then reads the sender from the status.

text: Process q sends and process r receives. The receive matches only if both use the same {{c1::communicator}} and the same {{c2::tag}}, the send's dest is r, and the receive's source is {{c3::q}}.
extra: The study guide says communicator, source and tag must all agree. If any one differs, the receive never completes.

text: Only the {{c1::receiver}} can use a wildcard such as \(\mathrm{MPI\_ANY\_TAG}\). The sender always names a rank and a tag, so MPI uses a {{c2::push}} mechanism. There is no wildcard for the {{c3::communicator}}.
extra: The two receive wildcards are \(\mathrm{MPI\_ANY\_SOURCE}\) and \(\mathrm{MPI\_ANY\_TAG}\).

text: A tag is a {{c1::nonnegative int}} that tells apart messages that are otherwise identical, for example floats to print versus floats to use in a computation.
extra: Process 1 can send the floats to print with tag 0 and the floats for the computation with tag 1.

text: In A2 the tag gives the message's purpose and the buffer carries the payload. The manager answers each worker request with {{c1::\(\mathrm{TAG\_WORK}\)}} and a ciphertext, or with {{c2::\(\mathrm{TAG\_STOP}\)}} once the batch is empty.
extra: Workers send \(\mathrm{TAG\_REQUEST}\) with a count, then one \(\mathrm{TAG\_RESULT}\) message per valid decryption.

text: Messages from one sender to one receiver are {{c1::non-overtaking}}, so they arrive in the order they were sent. Messages from different senders have {{c2::no guaranteed order}}.
extra: MPI cannot control network speed. If q runs on Mars and t runs on the same machine as r, q's earlier message may still arrive after t's.

text: \(\mathrm{MPI\_Send}\) may {{c1::buffer}} the message and return, or {{c2::block}} until it can start transmitting. Which one happens depends on the MPI implementation.
extra: Typical implementations buffer messages smaller than a cutoff size and block on larger ones.

text: When \(\mathrm{MPI\_Send}\) returns, you only know that the {{c1::send buffer can be reused}}. You do not know whether the message was transmitted.
extra: A buffered send returns as soon as MPI has copied the data and envelope into its own storage.

text: \(\mathrm{MPI\_Recv}\) {{c1::always blocks}} until a matching message arrives. So a receive with no matching send makes the process {{c2::hang}} forever.
extra: Lecture 9 says the number of sends and receives must be equal for this reason.

text: If the tag or rank in a receive doesn't match the intended send, the receiver may hang, or it may {{c1::match the wrong send}}.
extra: Pacheco calls the wrong match perhaps worse than a hang.

text: A send with no matching receive makes the sender {{c1::hang}} if \(\mathrm{MPI\_Send}\) blocks. If the send was buffered, the message is {{c2::lost}}.
Most MPI implementations let only {{c1::rank 0}} of \(\mathrm{MPI\_COMM\_WORLD}\) read stdin. That rank reads the input and {{c2::sends it to the other ranks}}.
extra: If several processes could read stdin, there would be no rule for which one gets which part of the input. A2 applies the same rule to input files.

text: Every rank may print to stdout, but the order of the lines is {{c1::nondeterministic}}, and one rank's output can {{c2::interrupt}} another's.
extra: The processes compete for stdout and MPI does not schedule access to it, so the order changes from run to run.

text: {{c1::\(\mathrm{MPI\_Init}\)}} sets up MPI and creates \(\mathrm{MPI\_COMM\_WORLD}\). No MPI call should come before it, and none after {{c2::\(\mathrm{MPI\_Finalize}\)}}.
extra: \(\mathrm{MPI\_Finalize}\) frees the resources MPI allocated.

text: You start 4 processes. Each one calls \(\mathrm{MPI\_Comm\_size}\) and gets {{c1::4}}. Each one calls \(\mathrm{MPI\_Comm\_rank}\) and gets its own rank, from {{c2::0 to 3}}.
extra: The rank plays the role of a process ID, but MPI keeps it system independent.

text: MPI programs are SPMD. You compile {{c1::one program}}, and each process {{c2::branches on its rank}} to do different work.
extra: SPMD means single program, multiple data. Write the program to run with any number of processes, because you rarely know the core count in advance.

text: Pthreads assumes {{c1::shared memory}} and works with threads. MPI assumes {{c2::distributed memory}} and works with {{c3::processes}}.
extra: MPI processes share nothing, so every piece of data a process needs must be sent to it explicitly.

text: A distributed memory system only makes sense when the machines spend more time {{c1::computing}} than {{c2::communicating}}.
extra: Sending data over the network takes much longer than sharing data between threads, so long data-parallel computations fit best.
